summary: A 35-ft steel Aermotor lookout placed in 1918 on Vanderwhacker Mountain in Essex County; fire watch ended in 1971 or 1988, and a 2005 article describes it as restored.

facts.agency: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation

staffing.status: unstaffed; fire watching ended in 1971 or 1988 depending on source

access.note: Vanderwhacker Mountain Wild Forest is open for recreation year-round and the Tower Trail reaches the summit. No current source confirms the cab is open to visitors, and Wikipedia reports an official closure in 1989.

visit.trail_note: 2.5-mile Tower Trail, about 1,650 ft of climbing from the Tower Trailhead; the road to the trailhead is often rough for low-clearance vehicles, and the NHLR suggests an extra 2.6-mile walk along it

events.note: Conservation Commission built a wooden fire observation tower on the mountain in May 1911 (Wikipedia)
Replaced by a 35-foot steel Aermotor LS40 tower; a new observer's cabin was built the same year
NHLR says the tower was staffed for fire spotting through 1971; this conflicts with the Wikipedia 1988 date
Wikipedia says fire watching stopped at the end of the 1988 season
Wikipedia says the NYS DEC officially closed the tower in early 1989
A September 2005 Lake Placid News article describes the tower as restored with a state Environmental Protection Fund grant; the year the work was done is not stated
Registered June 12, 2018 per the NHLR record

corrections.proposed: 1911 wooden tower built; 1918 steel tower replaced it
corrections.why: Wikipedia says the Conservation Commission built a wooden tower in May 1911 and replaced it in 1918; the NHLR gives only the 1918 date.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR says the tower was staffed for fire spotting through 1971; Wikipedia says fire watching stopped at the end of the 1988 season and the state closed it in early 1989. The story gives both and does not choose.

The state gives the summit as 3,386 ft; Wikipedia gives 3,389 ft (1,033 m); the NHLR gives the tower site as 3,325 ft (1,013 m), the figure in the brief. The story uses the state's 3,386 ft for the summit.
The NHLR uses Vandewhacker; the state and Wikipedia use Vanderwhacker. The story notes both spellings.

A hiking guide describes climbing the tower, but the state describes only the trail and the views from the cab, and Wikipedia reports an official closure in 1989. No source confirms the cab is open, so the story advises checking with the DEC before climbing.

notes_for_editor: The end of fire watch conflicts (1971 NHLR vs 1988 Wikipedia), and whether the cab is open to visitors is unconfirmed. Recommend a DEC check before the story is published as safe-to-visit. The brief's elevation (1,013.5 m) is the NHLR tower-site figure, not the summit. The AARCH item is a columnar newspaper PDF, so quotes are short fragments. Facebook group posts about the 1911 wood tower were not used. The Andy Arthur page was not used. No photo added.
